Pronunciation note for this grammar point:
The stress falls on the time marker, which is what makes the mix audible: I would BE there NOW; it would not HAVE happened.
Read it aloud, then record yourself: the main stress falls on the content word, not on the hedge.

elements.content: Grammar focus: Mixed Conditionals.

Choose the tense of each half by the time it refers to, not by the other half. If the condition is past and the result is now: if + past perfect, would + base. If the condition is now and the result is past: if + past simple, would have + participle. Never put would in the if-clause.

past condition + present result — if + past perfect, would + base: if I had taken it, I would be there now
present condition + past result — if + past simple, would have + participle: if she were careful, it would not have happened
past condition + past result — third conditional: if I had known, I would have called
present condition + present result — second conditional: if I knew, I would tell you
unreal past trait — were for all persons: if he were here
inverted form — Had / Were / Should + subject: had I taken the job, I would be in Berlin
Guided practice: choose the correct option.
1. Complete: 'If they had left earlier, they ___ here by now.'
2. Complete: 'If I ___ the answer, I would have told you.'
3. Which sentence is correct?
options: If I knew, I would have said it yesterday.
If I would know, I would say.
If I knew, I would say.

elements.content: Read and listen: three examples in context.

If I had studied medicine — I would be a doctor now. (Past condition, present result.)
If she were not so stubborn — she would have accepted the offer. (Present condition, past result.)
If they had invested in 2019 — they would own the market today. (Same form, different decades.)
What do you observe?

A mixed conditional joins two time frames. Past condition with present result: if + past perfect, would + base verb (If I had taken the job, I would be in Berlin now). Present condition with past result: if + past simple, would have + participle (If she were more careful, the error would not have happened). The condition and the result do not have to share a time.
1. In 'If I had taken the job, I would be in Berlin now', when is the result?
2. Which half is hypothetical in 'If she were more careful, the error would not have happened'?
options: The condition: she is not careful.
The result: the error did happen.

elements.content: State the rule in one sentence, without looking at the table.
Freer production: I can discuss consequences of different decisions.

Success criteria:
- I can keep the two halves of a conditional in different times.
- I can use were for an unreal present condition.
- I can invert a conditional instead of using if.
Role play: put your position in ninety seconds; your partner notes every use of the target structure.
Frequent errors and correction:

❌ If I would have taken the job, I would be in Berlin (would in the if-clause) → ✅ If I had taken the job, I would be in Berlin
❌ If she was more careful, the error would not have happened (indicative for an unreal present) → ✅ If she were more careful, the error would not have happened
Correct these sentences: say what is wrong, then give the right version.
Acceptable variants:

If we had kept the factory, the town would still have work.
If he were better organised, the deadline would have been met.
Had the warning been heeded, we would not be in this position.
Adapt the same task to the group:

- Individual: five sentences with the structure, on the topic of the lesson.
- Pair: a ten-line dialogue where conditional inversion carries the argument.
- Group: a six-minute debate, two sides, the structure required in every turn.
- Professional audience: transpose the structure into a memo.
- Academic audience: transpose it into a paragraph of analysis.
